gd.research.title: How to use TerraOrb for Researchers
gd.research.intro: This guide is for judges, students and researchers who want to check how TerraOrb works, including where it does not work well. Start with "How it works", then open "Method and data" for the tests and the files.
gd.research.method.name: The method
gd.research.method.what: The idea in plain words: how satellite measurements become advice for a tank, where the data comes from, and how far you can trust it.
gd.research.method.step1: Open "How it works" from the menu.
gd.research.method.step2: Read "From space to your field" for the four steps.
gd.research.method.step3: Read "Where the data comes from". Anything not from NASA is labelled "Not NASA".
gd.research.method.step4: Read "What to keep in mind" for the limits.
gd.research.method.tip: The pictures and videos on that page were made with AI to illustrate the ideas. They are not photos of real places or real data.
gd.research.tests.name: Accuracy tests
gd.research.tests.what: The backtests exactly as the pipeline saved them: crop advice against simply guessing, the El Niño outlook, and the tank water model. Good and bad results are both shown.
gd.research.tests.step1: Open "Method and data" from the menu.
gd.research.tests.step2: Scroll to "Accuracy tests" and note the date the tests were run.
gd.research.tests.step3: Compare each result with its simple baseline: a green line beat the baseline, a red line did not.
gd.research.tests.step4: Scroll to "Known limits" and read the problems listed there.
gd.research.tests.tip: A red result means the method does not beat its simple baseline, so the app does not rely on it. Much of the crop-advice success is simply knowing the wet and dry seasons, and the 16-day forecast part cannot be tested because past forecasts were not saved. If a "Demo data" label shows, the numbers say nothing about real tanks.
gd.research.files.name: Data files
gd.research.files.what: The saved files the website reads, ready to download and check. They are plain JSON with the source written inside.
gd.research.files.step1: Open "Method and data" and scroll to "Data files".
gd.research.files.step2: Tap a file name, such as tanks.json, climatology.json or validation.json, to open or download it.
gd.research.files.step3: Read the short note beside each file to see what it holds.
gd.research.files.step4: For one tank, open its own file in the data folder: data/tank/<id>.json.
gd.research.files.tip: Check the source and the date written inside a file before you reuse a number. Files marked as demo are placeholders, not real measurements.
gd.research.datasets.name: Data used and NASA maps
gd.research.datasets.what: A table of what each part of the site uses and whether it is NASA data, plus country-level NASA fires, stored groundwater and a NASA map with layers.
gd.research.datasets.step1: Open "Method and data" and read the table "What the site uses".
gd.research.datasets.step2: Check the "NASA data?" column: Yes, Partly or No.
gd.research.datasets.step3: Scroll to "Country-level NASA data" for fires seen from space (NASA FIRMS) and stored water in the ground (NASA GRACE-FO).
gd.research.datasets.step4: On the map, tap the layers button (top right) to switch between NASA pictures such as flood water, cloud cover, rain from space (IMERG) and greenness.
gd.research.datasets.tip: Open-Meteo (forecast, live rain, rain outlook) and OpenStreetMap (tank names and places) are not NASA data. The groundwater figure is one coarse measurement (about 300 km) for the whole country, and map layers are pictures from NASA GIBS, not tank measurements.
gd.research.datasets.go: Open the data table and map
